title: Don’t get one-shotted: Use AI to test, review, merge, and deploy code — Tomas Reimers, Graphite
talk_summary: Graphite argues AI has accelerated code creation, making review/test/merge/deploy the bottleneck; their AI reviewer uses codebase/change-history context, summarizes and prioritizes changes, integrates CI/test failures, and tunes for high-signal actionable comments. The talk is mostly product positioning with few implementation details, but it offers measurable review-noise and acceptance targets.

takeaways.what_they_do: They track whether AI review comments are accepted or dismissed and tune the reviewer to keep signal high and noise low.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We're watching our diamond comments be accepted about 52%.
takeaways.numbers: AI comments accepted ~52%; human comments integrated ~45-50%; AI comments downloaded at <4% rate

takeaways.technique: Codebase and change-history context for review
takeaways.what_they_do: The reviewer is designed to understand the codebase and prior change history rather than reviewing only the diff.
takeaways.evidence_quote: high signal low noise has a deep understanding of the codebase and change history

takeaways.technique: Summarize and prioritize each change before review
takeaways.what_they_do: They summarize and prioritize each change before reviewing it, so review effort is focused on what matters.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We summarize, prioritize and review each change

takeaways.what_they_do: They integrate with CI and testing infrastructure so the AI reviewer can summarize errors and correct failures.
Review comments are actionable and include one-click suggestions rather than only prose feedback.

takeaways.technique: AI-native outer loop, not just IDE/agents
takeaways.what_they_do: They argue the whole review/test/merge/deploy toolchain must be AI-native, not just code generation or isolated bots.
takeaways.evidence_quote: your entire tool chain has to be AI native, not just your IDE
